title: Introduction to Systems Biology
markdown: ## What this covers This is the opening lecture of MIT's *Systems Biology* (7.81J / 8.591J / 9.531J), and it answers two questions rather than developing any one piece of machinery: what does it mean to study biology as a *system* rather than gene by gene, and what does this particular course actually cover. It assumes nothing beyond the central dogma — DNA to RNA to protein — stated at the level given below. The chapter works through the semester's first real worked example, the decision a bacteriophage makes between killing its host and lying dormant inside it, and then previews, without deriving, the other case studies (bacterial chemotaxis and its adaptation, eukaryotic gradient sensing, the oscillation that finds the middle of a dividing cell, and the patterning of a fly embryo) that later lectures build up properly. Nothing here is meant to be complete; it is the map, plus the first stop on it. ## Systems biology as a discipline Take a network with several genes as inputs and some output behaviour: $$\text{gene A, gene B, \dots, gene F} \;\longrightarrow\; \text{OUTPUT}$$ Knowing the biochemical function of every gene product in detail does **not**, by itself, tell you the biological function of the network as a whole. That is the point of the field: a systems approach looks beyond any one gene or protein to ask what the pattern of feedbacks and feedforwards between them is *for* — what job the wiring does that no single component could do alone. In this course "systems biology" is used more or less interchangeably with "network biology": the goal is a quantitative understanding of the biological function of genetic and biochemical networks, not a catalogue of their parts. ## A map of the course The syllabus splits into three levels of complexity, each treating the cell (or the multicellular system) with a different level of spatial detail: **I. Systems microbiology** (14 lectures) — *the cell as a well-stirred biochemical reactor*, i.e. no spatial structure at all, only concentrations and rates: introduction (this lecture); chemical kinetics, equilibrium binding and cooperativity; the phage lambda switch; stability analysis; genetic switches; *E. coli* chemotaxis; fine-tuned versus robust models; receptor clustering; stochastic chemical kinetics; genetic oscillators; circadian rhythms. **II. Systems cell biology** (8 lectures) — *the cell as a compartmentalized system with concentration gradients*, where where things are inside the cell starts to matter: diffusion and Fick's equations; local-excitation/global-inhibition theory; models of eukaryotic gradient sensing; algorithms for finding the centre of a cell; cytoskeleton dynamics. **III. Systems developmental biology** (3 lectures) — *the cell in a social context, communicating with its neighbours*: quorum sensing; *Drosophila* development. This chapter sits at the very start of block I. The rest of it previews one worked picture from each of the three blocks — the phage switch in full, and sketches of chemotaxis, gradient sensing, cell polarity, and fly patterning — before the course commits to any one of them. ## The vocabulary: DNA, RNA, protein, and everything else The central dogma — $$\text{DNA} \xrightarrow{\text{replication}} \text{DNA}, \qquad \text{DNA} \xrightarrow{\text{transcription}} \text{mRNA}, \qquad \text{mRNA} \xrightarrow{\text{translation}} \text{protein}$$ — defines three of the four classes of biopolymer this course is built from: DNA, the passive library; RNA, a passive intermediate; and proteins, the active workhorses that actually do the catalysis, transport and signalling. The fourth class is not a polymer at all: "small molecules" — sugars, hormones, vitamins, substrates — the things the workhorses act on. A sense of the scale involved: a human cell holds about $6 \times 10^9$ base pairs of DNA, which laid end to end is about 2 m of double helix per cell. With roughly $75 \times 10^{12}$ cells in a human body, the total DNA in one person stretches to about $150 \times 10^{12}$ m — around a thousand times the Sun–Earth distance. All of that is packed into a volume you can hold in your hands. Any systems-level account of the cell has to be quantitative about numbers like these, not just about which gene talks to which. ## Case study I: the phage lambda switch Bacteriophage lambda is a virus with a genome of 48,512 base pairs. Once it injects its DNA into an *E. coli* host, the host's own transcription and translation machinery expresses the phage's genes — and *which* phage genes get expressed decides the phage's fate: **lysis** (make new phage particles and kill the host to release them) or **lysogeny** (integrate into the host genome and sit dormant, replicating along with the host indefinitely). This lysis/lysogeny decision is the course's first worked example of a genetic switch, and it is discussed here (and reproduced, with its images, from Ptashne's *A Genetic Switch: Phage Lambda*, the standing reference for this material throughout the lecture). ### The operator and its two promoters The decision is made at a short stretch of DNA called the right operator, $O_R$, which sits between two promoters running in opposite directions: $P_{RM}$, which transcribes the repressor gene $cI$ leftward, and $P_R$, which transcribes $cro$ rightward. $O_R$ itself is not one binding site but three, $O_R1$, $O_R2$ and $O_R3$, positioned so that RNA polymerase at $P_R$ overlaps the $O_R1/O_R2$ end of the operator and RNA polymerase at $P_{RM}$ overlaps the $O_R3$ end: Because the two promoters overlap different ends of the same three-site operator, a single kind of molecule — a repressor dimer, the product of the $cI$ gene itself — can act as a negative regulator of one promoter and a positive regulator of the other, depending on *which* site it sits on. The slides work through three cases: | Dimer occupying | Effect on $P_R$ (cro) | Effect on $P_{RM}$ (cI) | | --- | --- | --- | | $O_R2$ | blocks RNAp — negative control of cro | helps RNAp bind — positive control of cI | | $O_R1$ | blocks RNAp — negative control of cro | too far from $P_{RM}$ to act there* | | $O_R3$ | RNAp at $P_R$ unaffected — cro stays inducible | blocks RNAp — negative control of cI | \* the lecture's own phrasing for this case ("inhibits... too distant") is not fully consistent in the recovered notes; the qualitative point — that $O_R1$ is far enough from $P_{RM}$ that it should not act on it directly — is the one to keep, and Ptashne's book is the place to check the mechanism in detail. Two things are worth pulling out of that table. First, occupying $O_R2$ is special: it represses $cro$ *and* activates $cI$ at the same time, which is exactly what a stable, self-maintaining lysogenic state needs — the repressor helps make more of itself. Second, occupying $O_R3$ is the opposite kind of special: it is a brake on $cI$'s own promoter, so once repressor is abundant enough to reach $O_R3$, it starts turning off its own synthesis. Put together, this is a negative-feedback loop on repressor level (via $O_R3$) riding on top of a positive-feedback loop on repressor's own promoter (via $O_R2$) — which is how, in the lysogenic state, the lecture notes that repressor concentration is "maintained at a constant level by negative feedback." ### Cooperative binding turns a dial into a switch The three operator sites do not bind repressor independently. Their intrinsic (uncooperative) association constants differ roughly tenfold at each step, $$K_{O_R1} \sim 10\, K_{O_R2} \sim 10\, K_{O_R3},$$ so on affinity alone a dimer would fill $O_R1$ first, then $O_R2$, then $O_R3$ as concentration rises. But the *effective* affinity of $O_R2$ once $O_R1$ is already occupied, $K_{O_R2}^{*}$, is much larger than its intrinsic affinity $K_{O_R2}$ — a second dimer binding next to a first one gets a cooperative boost, presumably through direct dimer–dimer contact. This is why the switch is sharp rather than graded: a single, non-cooperative repressor–operator pair gives a shallow curve of percent repression against repressor concentration (Hill coefficient $n_H = 1$), while stacking two layers of cooperativity — monomers first have to dimerize, and then dimers cooperate across adjacent operator sites (giving something more like $n_H = 3$ in the comparison the lecture draws) — turns that shallow curve into a steep one. At the lysogen's actual repressor concentration the real system reaches about 99.7% repression: not "mostly off," but essentially digitally off. The point of building in several layers of cooperativity is precisely to convert what would otherwise be a graded chemical equilibrium into a well-defined, switch-like decision. ### Flipping the switch: UV induction The lysogenic state is stable, but not permanently locked. UV radiation triggers the SOS DNA-damage response, and one consequence is that the protein RecA becomes a protease specific for the lambda repressor. RecA cleaves repressor monomers; cleaved monomers can no longer dimerize; so the pool of repressor *dimers* — the only form that binds the operator — falls. As dimers vacate the operator, eventually all repressor leaves the DNA, $cro$ switches on, and the cell commits to lysis. It is worth noticing what the cooperativity from the previous section buys here: proteolysis acts on monomers, a comparatively gentle, linear removal process, but because the *bound*, lysogeny-holding state depends on two dimerization events and cooperative binding at two sites, a modest fall in monomer concentration is amplified into an abrupt collapse of operator occupancy — the same mechanism that makes the lysogenic state sharply "on" also makes it flip sharply to "off" once repressor synthesis can no longer keep pace with degradation. ## Case study II: *E. coli* chemotaxis and adaptation The second worked example previews lecture 7 and the block around it. Where the lambda switch is a question about a static decision made once, chemotaxis is a question about a decision network that runs continuously and must sense a changing environment. ### Running, tumbling, and sensing a gradient in time *E. coli* alternates between two modes of swimming: **running** (smooth, forward, flagella rotating in a bundle) and **tumbling** (flagella splay apart, the cell reorients randomly). Absent any chemical gradient, runs and tumbles alternate at a fixed baseline rate, and the net effect over time is an unbiased random walk — ordinary diffusion. In the presence of an attractant gradient (aspartate, in the experiments referenced), the same run/tumble machinery is *biased*: the cell suppresses tumbling while it happens to be swimming up-gradient, which turns the random walk into a walk biased toward the attractant source. The key phrase the lecture attaches to this is **temporal** sensing: the cell is far too small to compare concentration across its own length, so instead it compares the concentration it experiences *now* to the concentration it experienced a few seconds ago, as it swims. (This is contrasted, in the eukaryotic-chemotaxis preview later in the lecture, with cells large enough to sense a gradient *spatially*, across their own body — see below.) ### The signalling pathway The molecular pathway linking the receptor to the flagellar motor is a two-component signalling system (following Falke et al.'s review of the pathway): - attractants such as aspartate, serine and citrate bind the chemoreceptor directly; others (maltose, galactose, glucose, ribose, a dipeptide, Ni(II)) are first captured by a periplasmic binding protein that then engages the receptor; - the receptor, together with the adaptor CheW, forms a complex with CheA, a histidine kinase that autophosphorylates using ATP; - the phosphoryl group is passed from CheA to CheY, the response regulator that talks directly to the flagellar motor, and to CheB, a methylesterase that only acts on the receptor once phosphorylated; - CheZ dephosphorylates CheY-P, resetting the output arm; - CheR continually adds methyl groups to the receptor; CheB (only when phosphorylated) removes them. The receptor itself carries several methylation sites, and that methylation state is the variable that gives the system its memory. ### Adaptation: a response that resets itself The experiment the lecture uses to motivate the model tracks receptor methylation alongside behaviour through four phases: a baseline of steady tumbling and a fixed methylation level; then attractant is added — tumbling ceases almost immediately, and methylation begins to climb; then more attractant is added — methylation climbs further, to a new, higher plateau; then attractant is removed — tumbling increases (overshooting the original baseline) before resetting, and methylation falls back down. Behaviour reacts fast and transiently; methylation reacts slowly and tracks the stimulus level: The lecture writes this out as a small set of reactions on three time scales. **Fast** (effectively at equilibrium on the time scale of everything else): ligand binding to the receptor at any methylation and phosphorylation state, $T_m \rightleftharpoons LT_m$ for each $m$. **Slow**: sequential methylation of the receptor by CheR, $T_2 \to T_3 \to T_4$ (and the same for the ligand-bound and phosphorylated forms). **Intermediate**: phosphorylation of the receptor itself, $T_m \rightleftharpoons T_{mp}$. And two downstream output reactions, in which the phosphorylated, ligand-bound receptor hands its phosphate to the two response proteins: $$LT_{np} + Y \;\rightarrow\; Y_p + LT_n, \qquad LT_{np} + B \;\rightarrow\; B_p + LT_n.$$ The separation of time scales is the whole mechanism: ligand binding and phosphorylation are fast enough to produce an almost instantaneous drop in kinase activity (and hence in tumbling) when attractant appears, while methylation is slow enough that it only catches up afterward — and once it does, it pushes activity, and tumbling, back toward the pre-stimulus baseline even though the attractant is still there. The lecture poses the resulting question directly, and leaves it open for later lectures to answer: *what is the simplest mathematical model that is consistent with the biology and reproduces these experiments?* (citing Spiro, Parkinson and Othmer's 1997 model of excitation and adaptation in bacterial chemotaxis as the reference the figure is drawn from). ## Previews of what's ahead The rest of the lecture is a trailer for the two later blocks of the course, one picture from each, without derivation. **Eukaryotic gradient sensing (block II).** Where *E. coli* senses a gradient temporally, a eukaryotic cell such as the social amoeba *Dictyostelium* — for which cyclic AMP (cAMP) is the attractant — is large enough to sense it *spatially*, across its own body, and the response is qualitatively different: a uniform step increase in cAMP produces only a uniform, transient response, while a real spatial gradient produces a response confined to a leading-edge arc that persists as long as the gradient does: | | uniform step in cAMP | cAMP gradient | | --- | --- | --- | | response | uniform, all around the perimeter | confined to a leading-edge arc | | over time | transient — decays away | persistent — polarized, maintained | The lecture sketches a candidate molecular network behind this: a membrane lipid-signalling module (PI, PI4P, PIP2, PA, DG, IP3, and the enzymes converting between them, with transport of inositol through the endoplasmic reticulum) that includes a positive feedback loop, in which the product PA enhances the enzyme (PI4P5K) that makes more of the lipid upstream of it. **Finding the middle of a cell (block II).** In dividing *E. coli*, the site of division is set by an oscillation of the Min proteins: a tube of MinC/D, with a ring of MinE at its rim, forms and then moves from a central position toward one pole until it vanishes there, while a new tube and ring form in the other half of the cell — a full pole-to-pole cycle taking about 50 seconds. (More recent results, noted on the slide, show the Min proteins assembling into helices.) **Patterning a fly embryo (block III).** In *Drosophila*, each stripe visible in the early embryo corresponds to a specific body part in the adult fly, which is why the embryo is such a convenient system to study patterning in. A concentration gradient of the maternal protein bicoid is interpreted by the embryo's own (zygotic) gene expression — in particular, the gene hunchback reads out the bicoid gradient — to set up those stripes and, eventually, the body plan. ## Exercises The following are drawn from Problem Set 1 of the course's 2014 offering, and cover the modelling toolkit — gene expression reactions, dilution by growth, cooperative binding under detailed balance, and Michaelis–Menten kinetics — that this lecture's case studies draw on. **1. Transcription and translation.** Consider the reactions $$G \xrightarrow{\beta_g} G + M, \qquad M \xrightarrow{\alpha_m} \varnothing, \qquad M \xrightarrow{\beta_m} M + X,$$ $$X + S \underset{k_{1-}}{\overset{k_{1+}}{\rightleftharpoons}} X_S, \qquad X_S \underset{k_{2-}}{\overset{k_{2+}}{\rightleftharpoons}} X_S^{*},$$ where $G$ is the gene coding for protein $X$, $M$ is the mRNA transcribed from $G$, $S$ is a signalling molecule, $X_S$ is $X$ bound by $S$, and $X_S^{*}$ is the active form of $X$. a. For each reaction, say in words what step of gene expression or signalling it describes. b. Write the differential equations for the time evolution of $G$, $M$ and $X$ (do not forget to include the gene concentration itself in these equations). c. Using typical rate values for bacteria and for mammalian cells, indicate the typical time scale of each reaction in the two settings. d. Now suppose transcription of $G$ only occurs when its promoter is bound by the active form $X^{*}_S$, so the first reaction above is no longer valid on its own. Write the set of reactions describing promoter binding and transcription under this assumption. **2. Dilution of proteins due to cell growth.** A single bacterial cell at $t=0$ has volume $V_0$. After one doubling time $T_D$ it has grown and divided into two cells of volume $V_0$ each; after another $T_D$, four cells; and so on. a. Show that the combined volume of all cells at time $t$ can be written $V(t) = V_0 e^{\gamma t}$, and find $\gamma$ in terms of $T_D$. b. Protein $X$ is produced at some rate $k(t)$, so the total copy number satisfies $\frac{dn}{dt} = k(t)$. Show that the concentration $[X] = n/V$ obeys $\frac{d[X]}{dt} = \frac{k(t)}{V} - \gamma[X]$, and explain in words where the decay term comes from. c. Add active protein degradation, $X \xrightarrow{\delta} \varnothing$, to the equation from (b), and find the steady-state protein concentration. d. The same model applies to mRNA. Find, for an organism or cell type of your choice, its doubling time and the production and degradation rates of a favourite protein and mRNA, and use them to estimate steady-state protein and mRNA concentration. Give your sources. **3. Binding kinetics, detailed balance and cooperation.** A DNA segment $D$ has two sites, A and B, to which a protein $X$ can bind in either order, giving four dissociation constants $K_1, K_2, K_3, K_4$ for the two possible binding paths to the doubly-bound state $DX_AX_B$. a. Write the two expressions for the equilibrium ratio $[DX_AX_B]/([D][X]^2)$ that detailed balance gives via the two paths. Can all four constants be chosen independently? b. With total DNA concentration $[D_{\text{tot}}] = [D] + [DX_A] + [DX_B] + [DX_AX_B]$, show that if $K_1 \gg K_2$ and $K_3 \gg K_4$, the singly-bound forms are a negligible fraction of $[D_{\text{tot}}]$ — i.e. that this is a highly cooperative binding regime. c. Under that same approximation, find the bound fraction $f = [DX_AX_B]/[D_{\text{tot}}]$ as a function of $[X]$ and the dissociation constants. Sketch $f$ against $[X]$ and say what features of the sketch justify calling this binding "cooperative," compared to a non-cooperative interaction. **4. Michaelis–Menten kinetics.** Consider $E + S \underset{k_{1-}}{\overset{k_{1+}}{\rightleftharpoons}} ES \xrightarrow{k_2} E + P$, with initial concentrations $[E]=0.01$, $[S]=1$, $[ES]=0$, $[P]=0$ and rates $k_{1+}=1$, $k_{1-}=0.1$, $k_2=0.001$. a. Assuming the first reaction is much faster than the second ($k_{1+}, k_{1-} \gg k_2$), find the quasi-equilibrium concentration of $[ES]$. b. Estimate when the first reaction reaches quasi-equilibrium. c. Estimate the time at which substrate concentration has fallen to half its initial value. d. Simulate the full reaction scheme numerically from $t=0$ to $t=100{,}000$; compare the simulated production rate of $P$ as a function of $[S]$ to the Michaelis–Menten expression $V = V_{\max}S/(K_m+S)$, and identify where and why the two disagree, including at substrate concentrations close to the initial value. ## Sources - Slides: `lectures/01-notes.pdf` (2004 offering), split across three converted files — the course overview and syllabus, the central dogma and phage lambda introduction ([`01-7-81j-8-591j-9-531j.md`](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-591j-systems-biology-fall-2004/)); the three-case operator table, cooperative binding, UV induction, and the *E. coli* chemotaxis pathway ([`02-single-repressor-dimer-bound---three-cases.md`](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-591j-systems-biology-fall-2004/)); and the receptor-methylation adaptation experiment, plus the previews of eukaryotic gradient sensing, Min oscillation and *Drosophila* patterning ([`03-adaptation.md`](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-591j-systems-biology-fall-2004/)). These three files were converted by a model from a PDF with no text layer and are flagged in the source itself as "reconstructed" with "every equation unverified" — the qualitative structure (which promoter each operator site overlaps, the direction of cooperativity, the four adaptation phases) is used here with confidence, but exact numeric values and the ambiguous $O_R1$/$P_{RM}$ wording noted in the text should be checked against the cited primary sources before being relied on for anything quantitative. - Exercises: Problem Set 1, questions 1–4, 2014 offering (`psets/01-questions/01`–`04`). - No transcript or written notes were supplied for this lecture. - Not used here: the 2014 Exam #1 and its "network growth" question, also supplied as candidate exercises for this chapter. Both test material from much later in the syllabus — network motifs, feed-forward loops, the master equation, stochastic protein bursts, response times of simple circuits — none of which this lecture introduces, so they are left for the chapters that do. - Referred to but not supplied, and not reproduced beyond what is cited above: Mark Ptashne, *A Genetic Switch: Phage Lambda* (3rd ed., 2004) — the standing reference for the operator mechanism and its figures, cited on nearly every slide of the phage lambda section; Alberts et al., *Molecular Biology of the Cell* — the course's suggested background biology text; Falke, Bass, Butler, Chervitz and Danielson, "The two-component signaling pathway of bacterial chemotaxis," *Annu. Rev. Cell Dev. Biol.* 13 (1997) — source of the chemotaxis pathway diagram; Spiro, Parkinson and Othmer, "A model of excitation and adaptation in bacterial chemotaxis," *PNAS* 94 (1997) — source of the adaptation figure and the model the lecture's closing question points toward; Mittal, Budrene, Brenner and van Oudenaarden, "Motility of *Escherichia coli* cells in clusters formed by chemotactic aggregation," *PNAS* 100 (2003) — source of a chemotaxis image.
